passage: Ira's charts were the best in the group, and when she presented them Anand felt a sour twist. He had almost hidden his own rough draft until he asked her how she chose the colours; she showed him in five minutes, and he finished his section properly. In the meeting, Anand and Salma disagreed hotly: he wanted a survey, she wanted interviews. They agreed to test both on ten respondents each, and when the data favoured interviews and the group voted for that plan, Anand nodded and kept working without sulking. He handed Salma the results table and said, "Can you show me a draft on Wednesday and again on Friday?" When the draft arrived he said, "The layout is clear. The second column needs labels." On the last night the library closed at nine, so they moved to a canteen table, and Salma stayed until midnight helping him fix his broken references. Anand said, "You saved my grade. Thank you, truly. Send me your slides on Monday." On Monday he formatted her section without being asked.

qa.q: How many respondents did the group test each method on?
qa.a: They tested both methods on ten respondents each.

qa.q: How did Anand's reaction to Ira's charts differ from his reaction when the data favoured Salma's plan?
qa.a: With Ira's charts he felt a sour twist of envy but chose to learn from her instead of hiding his work; when the data favoured interviews and the group voted, he accepted the decision and kept working without sulking.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling when Ira presented her charts?
qa.a: He felt envious, a sour twist, because her work was better than his.

qa.q: What could Anand do next to return Salma's help?
qa.a: He could offer her help in return, as he did by formatting her section, and keep thanking her for staying late.

grounding: Four moments in one student group project show envy of a star, a disagreement settled by data, hand-over with checkpoints and gratitude for late help.
